rationale: A wins because it keeps the knife on the facts: "Replit charges by usage for an agent it won't say how often gets the app right" turns two supplied details into a clean reporter question. B has real instincts, but "You pay per build" invents a billing unit and "from one English sentence" tightens "plain-English description" into copywriter glitter. That is how a decent angle becomes a correction.
gaps_in_A: "The same product will land in the accounts schools already use" assumes the agent is enabled on education accounts; the update only says Replit is used heavily in education.
"Tens of millions of hobbyists would rather describe an app than code one" smuggles in "hobbyists" and user preference; the facts say non-engineers, vibe coders, and a company-claimed user count.
"Replit's agent built our apps. Here is how many ran without a fix." is a strong reviewer assignment, but weak founder-side pitching unless Replit can offer uncurated access and accept bad results.
gaps_in_B: "from one English sentence" is not in the update; the fact is a plain-English description, which could be much longer.
"You pay per build" is invented. Usage-based pricing could mean tokens, compute, deploys, runs, or something else; the proof section admits this after the headline already overclaims.
"The prevailing belief Replit is selling into" creates a market belief without evidence from the supplied update. A contrarian angle needs either the company's own explicit claim or outside proof.
"most students before a course, not after" is armchair education sociology. The angle needs a named instructor, course, or classroom policy, not a neat line about students who cannot code.
